50-30-20-budget.title: The 50/30/20 Budget: A Simple Plan That Actually Sticks
50-30-20-budget.excerpt: A budget only works if you can keep it up. The 50/30/20 rule is popular because it is simple: split your after-tax income into needs, wants, and savings.

blocks.text: Most budgets fail not because they are wrong, but because they are exhausting. The 50/30/20 rule works because it asks for awareness, not perfection. You divide your take-home pay into three buckets and adjust from there.
The three buckets

items: Needs (50%): rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, insurance, minimum debt payments.
Wants (30%): dining out, streaming, hobbies, travel, the things that make life feel good.
Savings (20%): emergency fund, retirement, and any extra debt payments.

blocks.text: Start by calculating your after-tax income. If you are not sure what lands in your account after deductions, our [Income Tax Calculator](/finance/income-tax) can estimate your net pay first.
Why it works

The rule forces the savings habit before spending, not with whatever is left over. Even a steady 20% rate builds a real cushion surprisingly fast, and the structure makes overspending obvious the moment a bucket overflows.
Automate the 20% transfer on payday so saving happens before you can spend it. Out of sight is the whole point.
When to adjust

In high-cost cities the split might need to be 60/20/20 for a while, and that is fine. The point is direction, not a rigid number. Use our [Savings Goal Calculator](/finance/savings-goal) to see how your 20% compounds over time.

compound-interest-early.title: Compound Interest: Why Starting Early Beats Saving More Later
compound-interest-early.excerpt: Albert Einstein supposedly called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Whether or not he said it, the math is real: your money earns returns, and then those returns earn returns.

blocks.text: Compounding is the quiet engine behind nearly every long-term financial goal. You invest money, it grows, and the growth itself starts earning more. The longer the runway, the more dramatic the effect.
The snowball effect

Run the numbers in our [Compound Interest Calculator](/finance/compound-interest): put 200 per month at 7% for 30 years and you will see that most of the final balance came from growth, not from your contributions.
Time beats amount

Investing 100 a month from age 25 often beats investing 300 a month from age 40. The early money compounds for an extra 15 years, and those years do the heavy lifting. This is why procrastination is the most expensive habit in personal finance.
The single biggest factor in compounding is starting time. You cannot recover lost years, no matter how much you add later.
Make it automatic
Pair compounding with consistency using a [Savings Goal Calculator](/finance/savings-goal). Set the target, set the date, and let regular contributions do the rest.

bmi-body-fat-explained.title: BMI, Body Fat, and What Your Weight Number Really Means
bmi-body-fat-explained.excerpt: Step on a scale and the number feels like a verdict. But weight alone hides more than it reveals. BMI is a starting point, not a finish line.

blocks.text: We tend to treat a single weight number as the whole story. It is not. Two people can weigh the same and have completely different bodies. The useful question is not just how much you weigh, but what that weight is made of.
What BMI actually measures

Body Mass Index is weight divided by height squared. It groups you as underweight, normal, overweight, or obese. It is a cheap, fast screen, and you can find your number with the [BMI Calculator](/health/bmi).
Where BMI falls short

Muscle weighs more than fat. A trained athlete can read as overweight while having very low body fat. That is why [Body Fat Calculator](/health/body-fat) and lean-mass estimates give a fuller picture than BMI alone.
Use BMI as a screen, not a diagnosis. Waist size and body composition usually tell the more honest story.
A healthier lens

Instead of fixating on the scale, combine your [BMR Calculator](/health/bmr-calculator) and [TDEE Calculator](/health/tdee-calculator) to understand your energy needs. Weight is a lagging indicator; energy balance is the thing you can actually steer.

extra-mortgage-payments.title: How Extra Mortgage Payments Save You Years of Interest
extra-mortgage-payments.excerpt: A 30-year mortgage is mostly interest in the early years. Small extra payments can shave years, and thousands of dollars, off the loan.

blocks.text: The first few years of a mortgage can feel discouraging: a large payment, but the balance barely moves. That is because early payments go mostly to interest. The good news is that extra payments hit the principal hardest exactly when it matters most.
How amortization works
Amortization front-loads interest. Our [Mortgage Calculator](/finance/mortgage) shows the split between principal and interest for every month, so you can see how slowly the balance falls at first.
The power of a small extra amount
On a typical loan, an extra 100 per month can cut four to six years off the term and save tens of thousands in interest. The sooner you start, the bigger the effect.
Always tell your lender the extra payment should go to principal, not toward future scheduled payments.
Compare the trade-off

Before throwing everything at the mortgage, weigh it against other goals using the [ROI Calculator](/finance/roi) and [Savings Goal Calculator](/finance/savings-goal). Sometimes a higher-return investment beats paying the loan early.

percentages-in-everyday-life.title: Percentages in Real Life: Discounts, Tips, and Tax Made Easy
percentages-in-everyday-life.excerpt: Percentages run the everyday math of money, from sales and tips to tax and interest. Once the pattern clicks, you can do most of it in your head.

blocks.text: Percent means per hundred. Anchor every percentage problem to 100 and most of them stop being intimidating. The same idea powers discounts, tips, tax, and growth.
Discounts

A 30% discount on an 80 item saves 24, leaving 56. The shortcut is price times (1 minus the rate). Our [Discount Calculator](/math/discount) does it instantly, but the mental version is handy at the register.
Tips
An 18% tip on a 50 bill is 9. The [Tip Calculator](/math/tip) handles groups and rounding, but here is the trick: 10% is easy to find, and 20% is simply double that.
Tax and growth
The same percentage logic describes interest and inflation. See how a rate compounds over time with the [Percentage Calculator](/math/percentage-calculator).
Percent literally means per hundred. Anchor every percentage problem to 100 and it gets simple fast.

calories-bmr-tdee.title: Calories, BMR, and TDEE: Planning a Diet That Actually Works
calories-bmr-tdee.excerpt: Eat less, move more is true but useless without numbers. Your calorie needs are personal, and two calculators explain why.

blocks.text: Generic diet advice ignores the fact that everyone burns a different amount of energy. The fix is to estimate your own numbers first, then build a plan around them.
BMR: your resting burn
Basal Metabolic Rate is the calories you burn at complete rest, just keeping you alive. Find yours with the [BMR Calculator](/health/bmr-calculator).
TDEE: your real daily need
Total Daily Energy Expenditure adds your activity on top of BMR. The [TDEE Calculator](/health/tdee-calculator) turns that into a daily target you can actually eat to.
Losing or gaining weight

A deficit of about 500 kcal per day is roughly one pound per week. Track your food with the [Calorie Calculator](/health/calorie-calculator) and your macros with the [Macro Calculator](/health/macro-calculator).
Crash diets drop water, not fat. Aim for a modest, sustainable deficit you can keep for months.

cooking-unit-conversions.title: Cooking Unit Conversions: Cups, Grams, and Ounces Without the Guesswork
cooking-unit-conversions.excerpt: A recipe calls for 200 g of flour but your cups are imperial. Converting cooking units should not ruin dinner.

blocks.text: Cooking across recipes from different countries means juggling cups, grams, ounces, and milliliters. The reliable move is to stop measuring by volume and start measuring by weight.
Weight beats volume
A cup of flour can vary by 20% depending on how you scoop it. Our [Cooking Units Converter](/cooking/cooking-units) handles cups, grams, ounces, and milliliters so your results stay consistent.
Scaling recipes

Doubling a recipe by hand is error-prone. The [Recipe Scaler](/cooking/recipe-scaler) adjusts every ingredient automatically, and the [Food Cost Calculator](/cooking/food-cost) prices it out if you are cooking for a crowd.
Flour and sugar are not interchangeable by volume. Always convert by weight when you bake.
Beyond the kitchen
For general measurements, the [Unit Converter](/math/unit-converter) covers length, temperature, and more when a recipe strays into non-cooking territory.

debt-snowball-vs-avalanche.title: Debt Snowball vs. Avalanche: Which Payoff Method Wins?
debt-snowball-vs-avalanche.excerpt: Two popular methods promise to crush debt. They differ on one question: do you pay by emotion, or by math?

blocks.text: If you carry several debts, the order you pay them off matters as much as the amount. The two best-known strategies attack that order very differently.
Snowball: motivation first

List debts smallest balance to largest. Pay the minimum on all, then throw every extra dollar at the smallest. Quick wins build momentum. Model the whole thing in our [Debt Snowball and Avalanche Calculator](/finance/debt-snowball-avalanche).
Avalanche: math first
Pay the highest interest rate first. You save the most money and finish fastest, but the early progress can feel slow because big balances linger.
Mathematically, avalanche wins. Behaviorally, snowball often sticks. Pick the one you will actually finish.
Do not forget the rate
Before choosing, compare the cost of your debt to what you might earn investing with the [ROI Calculator](/finance/roi). Sometimes it pays to invest while making minimum payments.

equal-installment-vs-principal.title: Equal Installment vs Equal Principal: Which Mortgage Saves More
equal-installment-vs-principal.excerpt: Same loan amount, same rate — yet the two repayment methods can differ by tens of thousands in total interest. Here's how to choose.

blocks.text: When you take out a mortgage, the bank usually asks you to pick between an equal-installment plan and an equal-principal plan. Monthly payments, total interest, and early-years burden all differ — yet many people sign without understanding the trade-off.
The core difference

items: Equal installment: a fixed monthly payment. Early payments are mostly interest; later payments shift toward principal.
Equal principal: a fixed monthly principal portion. Interest is charged on the remaining balance, so the payment shrinks every month.

blocks.text: Our [Loan Calculator](/finance/loan) makes it concrete: on a $1,000,000 loan over 30 years at 4%, equal installment costs about $4,774/month. Equal principal starts near $6,111/month and drops by roughly $11 each month.
How much interest is at stake

In that same example, equal installment totals about $719,000 in interest while equal principal totals about $602,000 — a gap of roughly $117,000. The difference comes from how fast the balance shrinks: equal principal cuts the interest-bearing base sooner.
So is equal principal always better?

Not necessarily. Its early payments run about 28% higher, which is real pressure for a household that just bought a home. If the extra monthly cost squeezes your lifestyle or pushes you toward credit-card debt, the interest you save isn't worth it.
A simple rule: if you can comfortably afford the higher early payments, choose equal principal. Otherwise take equal installment and use the savings to prepay the loan.
What if you plan to prepay?

If you expect to clear the loan within 5 to 10 years, the gap between the two methods narrows sharply, because much of the interest never accrues. Focus instead on prepayment penalties and on shortening the term rather than lowering the monthly payment. Compare scenarios with the [Mortgage Calculator](/finance/mortgage).

credit-card-minimum-payment-trap.title: The Real Cost of Paying Only the Credit Card Minimum
credit-card-minimum-payment-trap.excerpt: Paying the minimum feels manageable, but it's one of the most expensive ways to borrow. A few thousand in debt can take over a decade to clear.

blocks.text: When the statement arrives, the minimum is usually just 5% or 10% of the balance — it looks like a friendly buffer. In reality it's one of the card issuer's most profitable designs: the rest accrues daily interest, and the grace period usually disappears.
A concrete example

Say you owe $10,000 at 18% APR (about 0.05% per day) with a 10% minimum. You pay $1,000 the first month; the remaining $9,000 keeps accruing interest. Next month the minimum drops to $900, so you pay even less while interest keeps running.
Run it through the [Credit Card Calculator](/finance/credit-card): paying only the minimum, clearing that $10,000 can take more than 14 years and cost over $8,000 in interest.
Why the minimum is so expensive

items: The grace period vanishes: if you don't pay in full, interest is charged from the posting date of each purchase, not after 20–50 interest-free days.
Daily interest, monthly compounding: interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself.
The minimum keeps shrinking: as the balance falls, so does your payment, so principal barely moves.

blocks.text: Three cheaper alternatives

items: Pay in full: the only option with zero interest, and it should be your default.
Installment plans: they carry fees, but the rate is usually below revolving interest, with a fixed, predictable term.
Balance transfer or a low-rate loan: for large balances, compare the annual cost of a [personal loan](/finance/personal-loan).

blocks.text: The minimum should be an emergency stopgap, never a habit. Even $100 extra per month cuts years off the payoff.
How to get out fast

Stop adding new charges, then use the [Debt Snowball vs Avalanche Calculator](/finance/debt-snowball-avalanche) to set your order: avalanche (highest rate first) costs least overall, while snowball (smallest balance first) is easier to stick with.

emergency-fund-how-many-months.title: How Many Months of Expenses Should Your Emergency Fund Cover?
emergency-fund-how-many-months.excerpt: “Three to six months” is the standard advice, but that range hides the real question: your job stability and family structure decide the number.

blocks.text: Nearly every personal-finance book says to keep three to six months of expenses in reserve. The range is reasonable, but it glosses over the key issue: whether you need three months or six depends on your exposure to risk, not on an average.
What drives the number

items: Income stability: tenured or salaried roles vary little; freelancing, commission-based sales, and entrepreneurship vary a lot.
Job market: if your industry is hiring and you could re-employ quickly, you can hold less; if it's contracting, hold more.
Household structure: two incomes with no children is lowest risk; single-income households with children or dependents are higher.
Fixed obligations: the more you have in mortgage, car loans, and insurance that can't be paused, the bigger the buffer you need.
Existing safety nets: health insurance, unemployment benefits, and private coverage absorb part of the risk.

blocks.text: A workable rule of thumb

items: 3 months: two incomes, no children, healthy industry, stable social insurance.
6 months: single-income household, has a mortgage, average industry.
9–12 months: freelancer, founder, single parent, weak industry, or income heavily dependent on commission.

blocks.text: How to compute your number

The fund covers essential spending, not your full lifestyle. Add rent or mortgage, food, utilities, transport, insurance, and minimum debt payments to get your monthly baseline, then multiply by your target months. Use the [Savings Goal Calculator](/finance/savings-goal) to work out the monthly deposit needed.
An emergency fund is optimised for access, not return. Keep it in a savings account or money-market fund — not locked in a term deposit or volatile assets.
When to actually use it

Only genuine surprises qualify: job loss, serious illness, essential major repairs. Planned expenses — a new car, a holiday, a renovation — should be saved for separately and never eat into the buffer. After you dip in, refilling it becomes priority one.

inflation-purchasing-power.title: What Will Your $100 Buy in 10 Years? Inflation and Purchasing Power
inflation-purchasing-power.excerpt: Inflation doesn't shrink your money — it shrinks what your money can buy. Understanding that erosion is lesson one in why you invest.

blocks.text: Cash in a drawer doesn't lose its number — but ten years later it buys less. That is inflation eroding purchasing power: the most overlooked yet most certain risk in personal finance.
How to compute purchasing power
The formula is simple: future purchasing power = present amount ÷ (1 + inflation rate) ^ years. At 3% inflation, $100 today has the buying power of about $74 in ten years, and about $55 in twenty.
The [Inflation Calculator](/finance/inflation) shows the erosion across different rates and horizons.
Why this forces you to invest

items: Savings-account rates usually sit below inflation, so real returns are negative.
Even if your balance grows in nominal terms, if the return trails inflation your real purchasing power still falls.
Judge an investment by its real return: nominal return minus inflation.

blocks.text: 3% inflation sounds mild, but it means purchasing power halves in roughly 24 years. Simple arithmetic — and rarely done.

That said, fear of inflation is no reason to gamble blindly. Build your [emergency fund](/blog/emergency-fund-how-many-months) first, then put long-horizon money into assets with a chance of beating inflation, and model the outcome with the [Compound Interest Calculator](/finance/compound-interest).
Your income needs to keep up too

The income side is equally overlooked. If your salary hasn't moved in years, your real income has been shrinking. When weighing a job's long-term value, whether raises outpace inflation matters more than the current number.

apr-vs-apy-interest-rate-basics.title: Nominal Rate, Real Rate, and EAR: Don't Let the Numbers Fool You
apr-vs-apy-interest-rate-basics.excerpt: Is “12% per year” the same as “1% per month”? Not once compounding enters the picture — and the gap can be costly.

blocks.text: Loan ads love “0.5% per month.” Deposit products love “4% annualized.” Both look reasonable, but if you don't understand how interest is compounded, you'll underestimate true cost and overestimate true return.
Three terms you must separate

items: Nominal rate: the stated annual rate in the contract, ignoring compounding frequency.
Periodic rate: the rate per compounding period — monthly rate = nominal annual rate ÷ 12.
Effective annual rate (EAR/APY): the true annual cost or return once compounding is included.

blocks.text: How compounding frequency changes things

A 12% nominal rate compounded annually gives an EAR of 12%. Compounded monthly, the periodic rate is 1% and the true annual cost is (1 + 1%) ^ 12 − 1 ≈ 12.68%. Daily compounding pushes it higher still.
The gap looks small, but on a large balance over decades it is real money. Always convert products to a common basis before comparing.
One line to remember: compare loans by EAR and deposits by APY. A nominal rate is only directly comparable when compounding frequency matches.
Practical steps

When you get a quote, ask three things: what is the nominal annual rate, how often does it compound, and are there fees? Many “low-rate” products hide their true cost in fees. Enter different parameters in the [Loan Calculator](/finance/loan) to compare monthly payments and total cost.
For savings, use the [Compound Interest Calculator](/finance/compound-interest) to estimate actual returns at different compounding frequencies, so marketing language doesn't mislead you.

rent-vs-buy-decision.title: Rent or Buy? Run the Numbers Before You Decide
rent-vs-buy-decision.excerpt: “Buying always beats renting” is a popular claim, but the real answer depends on the price-to-rent ratio, how long you'll stay, and your city.

blocks.text: Few financial decisions are as emotionally loaded as renting versus buying. Elders say renting is “paying your landlord's mortgage”; agents say “buy early, gain early.” But this question can be settled with numbers instead of slogans.
Two metrics that matter

items: Price-to-rent ratio: home price ÷ annual rent. The lower, the better buying looks. Roughly, below 15 favors buying; above 25 favors renting.
Holding period: how long you plan to stay in the city. Transaction costs — taxes, agent fees, renovation — need years to amortize.

blocks.text: The true cost of buying is more than the mortgage

Many people compare only “mortgage vs rent,” which is incomplete. Buying also carries the opportunity cost of the down payment, maintenance fees, repairs, property taxes, and eventual selling costs. Renting costs the rent itself plus the opportunity cost of the deposit.

Use the [Mortgage Calculator](/finance/mortgage) for payments and total interest, then the [ROI Calculator](/finance/roi) to estimate what the down payment could earn if invested — and compare the two together.
When renting makes more sense

items: You'll stay in the city fewer than 3 to 5 years.
Your job or income is unstable and you need flexibility.
The local price-to-rent ratio is clearly high.
You can't afford a down payment without draining your emergency fund.

blocks.text: Remember: buying is not an investment; it's consumption plus forced savings. It gives you housing and discipline, but very poor liquidity and high transaction costs. Expecting investment-grade returns usually disappoints.
A middle path

Renting first is no disgrace. Accumulate a down payment, learn the city and neighborhood, confirm job stability — better than rushing in under pressure. Once you're sure you'll put down roots, model it carefully with the [Mortgage Calculator](/finance/mortgage).

bmi-limitations-better-metrics.title: BMI Isn't Enough: Why You Also Need Body Fat and Waist
bmi-limitations-better-metrics.excerpt: BMI summarizes everyone with one height-weight formula, so it inevitably misjudges muscular people and older adults. Know its blind spots to use it well.

blocks.text: BMI is a screening tool, not a diagnostic one. Its value is that it's cheap, fast, and works across large populations; its cost is that it is crude at the individual level.
Three main blind spots

items: It can't tell muscle from fat: two people at 80 kg — a bodybuilder and a sedentary office worker — can share the same BMI with completely different bodies.
It ignores fat distribution: visceral fat around the abdomen carries far more risk than subcutaneous fat in the limbs, and BMI sees none of this.
It overlooks age and sex: at the same BMI, older adults usually carry more fat than younger people, and women naturally carry more than men.

blocks.text: Two better additions

First, body fat percentage. It directly reflects how much of your body is fat, a far better health signal than weight. Estimate it with the [Body Fat Calculator](/health/body-fat). Home scales have error, but the long-term trend matters more than any single reading.
Second, waist circumference. It reflects abdominal fat and is a key warning sign for metabolic syndrome. Generally, risk rises above roughly 90 cm in men and 80 cm in women (China guidelines).
Treat BMI as a starting point, not a conclusion. If BMI says overweight but body fat and waist are fine, you probably just carry muscle. If BMI is normal but your waist is large, don't be complacent.
How to use it properly

Get an initial read from the [BMI Calculator](/health/bmi), then combine it with [body fat](/health/body-fat) and waist. Better still, watch the trend: whether these numbers rise or fall over six months says far more than one measurement.
One caveat: every online calculator is an estimate. If your numbers look abnormal or you have a medical condition, rely on an in-person doctor and clinical testing.

bmr-tdee-how-many-calories.title: BMR and TDEE: How Many Calories Should You Actually Eat?
bmr-tdee-how-many-calories.excerpt: Fat loss comes down to a calorie deficit — but a deficit relative to what you actually burn. BMR and TDEE answer that question.

blocks.text: There is no universal answer to “how much should I eat” — it depends on your body and your activity. BMR and TDEE are the two concepts that turn that question into numbers.
BMR: the calories you burn lying still

Basal metabolic rate is the minimum energy your body needs at complete rest, fasting, in a neutral-temperature environment. It accounts for 60–75% of daily burn. Estimate it with the [BMR Calculator](/health/bmr-calculator), which uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation.
TDEE: your true burn once activity counts

Total daily energy expenditure multiplies BMR by an activity factor: about 1.2 sedentary, 1.375 light, 1.55 moderate, 1.725 intense. The [TDEE Calculator](/health/tdee-calculator) gives you the number directly.

items: Sedentary (desk job, little exercise): BMR × 1.2
Light (training 1–3 days/week): BMR × 1.375
Moderate (training 3–5 days/week): BMR × 1.55
Intense (training 6–7 days/week): BMR × 1.725

blocks.text: How to plan your intake
To lose fat: subtract 300–500 kcal from TDEE daily, which theoretically yields about 0.3–0.5 kg per week. To build muscle: add 200–400 kcal above TDEE with adequate protein.
Don't cut intake below BMR for long periods. Severe restriction slows metabolism and breaks down muscle, making fat loss harder and rebound very likely.
Use the [Macro Calculator](/health/macro-calculator) to split protein, carbs, and fat — easier to sustain and healthier than chasing calories alone.
The calculator is a starting point

Equations carry individual error, sometimes around 10%. The practical method: start with the estimate, run it for two weeks, then adjust based on the scale. If weight hasn't moved, trim another 100–200 kcal.

daily-water-intake-guide.title: How Much Water Should You Drink? Calculate by Weight, Not by “8 Glasses”
daily-water-intake-guide.excerpt: “Eight glasses a day” is catchy, but a 50 kg person and a 90 kg person clearly don't need the same. Weight and activity are better guides.

blocks.text: “Drink eight glasses (about 2 liters) a day” is everywhere, but it's a rounded, rough guideline that ignores the variables that matter most: body weight, climate, and activity.
Calculate from body weight

A common estimate: daily water in ml = body weight in kg × 30 to 35. A 60 kg adult needs roughly 1,800–2,100 ml per day. The [Water Intake Calculator](/health/water-intake) gives you a personalized number.
When you need more

items: Exercise and sweat: add roughly 500–700 ml per hour of activity.
Heat or humidity: sweat losses rise sharply, so intake should follow.
High altitude or dry aircraft cabins: water is lost faster through breathing and skin.
Fever, diarrhea, or vomiting: losses accelerate, so replace fluids and electrolytes promptly.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: needs rise clearly — confirm the amount with your doctor.

blocks.text: Water isn't only plain water

Many assume only plain water counts. In reality food counts too — fruits and vegetables are often over 90% water — as do soup, milk, tea, and coffee. Coffee's mild diuretic effect offsets part of its fluid, but it doesn't cause a net loss.
The simplest adequacy check is urine color: pale yellow means well hydrated, dark yellow means drink more, and completely clear may mean too much.
More isn't always better

Water is not the more the better. Drinking very large amounts quickly can cause hyponatremia, which is rare but can be life-threatening. People with kidney failure or heart failure need doctor-set fluid limits and shouldn't apply a generic formula.

waist-circumference-health-risk.title: Waist Circumference: A Better Risk Predictor Than Weight
waist-circumference-health-risk.excerpt: Where your fat sits matters more than how much you carry. Abdominal fat is directly tied to heart disease and diabetes, and waist is the easiest way to measure it.

blocks.text: Two people can have identical weight and BMI yet vastly different risk profiles — the difference is where the fat is stored. Visceral fat around the abdomen releases inflammatory signals and disrupts metabolism, making it far riskier than fat under the skin of the limbs.
How to measure it correctly

items: Timing: in the morning, fasting, after emptying your bladder, standing and breathing normally.
Position: a common method is the midpoint between the lower rib margin and the top of the hip bone (usually navel level); the WHO suggests the midpoint between the lower rib and the iliac crest.
Technique: the tape sits on the skin without compressing it; read at the end of a normal exhalation, to the nearest 0.1 cm.
Cautions: don't suck in your stomach, and don't measure right after a large meal.

blocks.text: Reference thresholds

items: Men: ≥ 90 cm indicates abdominal (central) obesity.
Women: ≥ 80 cm indicates abdominal obesity.
Above these levels, the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease rises markedly.

blocks.text: These are commonly used thresholds; different countries and bodies vary slightly. Pair the reading with the [BMI Calculator](/health/bmi) — using both together gives a more reliable picture.
Waist measurement's advantage: no equipment, a few seconds, and it often predicts risk better than BMI.
What to do if your waist is high

The good news is that visceral fat responds readily to lifestyle change. Cutting refined carbohydrates and added sugar, adding aerobic exercise, protecting sleep, and drinking less alcohol all shrink abdominal fat. Note that spot reduction is a myth — the body mobilizes fat overall, and the abdomen usually changes first.
Tracking with the [Body Fat Calculator](/health/body-fat) and waist-to-hip measures such as those in [body type](/health/body-type) is far more informative than watching the scale alone.

percentage-increase-decrease-guide.title: Percent Increase and Decrease: Mind the Base
percentage-increase-decrease-guide.excerpt: Up 50% then down 50% doesn't bring you back to the start. Understanding the base-rate trap prevents a lot of mistakes in investing and shopping.

blocks.text: Percentages are among the most commonly miscalculated things in daily life, and the cause is almost always the same: using the wrong base.
The basic formulas

items: Change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100%
New = original × (1 + increase%)
Original = new ÷ (1 + increase%)

blocks.text: The second line is the crux: a percentage is always relative to the original value. Verify quickly with the [Percentage Calculator](/math/percentage-calculator).
The classic trap: gains and losses aren't symmetric
Say a stock goes from $100 to $150 — a 50% gain. It then falls from $150 back to $100. That drop is (100 − 150) ÷ 150 = −33.3%, not −50%. Same $50 move, but the base shifted from 100 to 150.
Up 50% then down 50% leaves you at 100 × 1.5 × 0.5 = 75 — a 25% loss. That asymmetry is the cost.
Another trap: percentage points vs percent

If a rate rises from 4% to 5%, you can say it rose “1 percentage point” or that it rose 25% — (5 − 4) ÷ 4. Both are correct but mean different things, and news coverage mixes them to exaggerate. Always check which one is meant.
Practical cases

items: Discounts: 20% off means paying 80% of the original price.
Tipping: a 15% tip on a $200 bill comes to 200 × 1.15 = $230.
Tax-inclusive prices: at a 5% tax rate, pre-tax = tax-inclusive ÷ 1.05 — not multiplied by 0.95.
Investment return: (sale price − purchase price + dividends) ÷ purchase price × 100%.

blocks.text: For more tax and discount scenarios, use the [Discount Calculator](/finance/discount) and the [Percentage Calculator](/math/percentage-calculator).

common-unit-conversion-mistakes.title: Where Unit Conversions Most Often Go Wrong
common-unit-conversion-mistakes.excerpt: Feet and inches to centimeters? Pounds to kilos? How many gallons are there? Most conversion errors aren't arithmetic — they're the wrong definition.

blocks.text: Unit conversion looks like plain multiplication and division, but the vast majority of mistakes aren't arithmetic slips. They come from using the wrong factor or confusing units that share a name.
Trap 1: feet and inches aren't decimal

5 feet 8 inches is often misread as 5.8 feet. The correct approach is to divide the inches by 12 and add: 5 + 8 ÷ 12 = 5.667 feet, then multiply by 30.48 to get about 172.7 cm. A conversion tool avoids the manual arithmetic entirely.
Trap 2: there are three gallons

items: US gallon ≈ 3.785 L
Imperial (UK) gallon ≈ 4.546 L
US dry gallon ≈ 4.405 L

blocks.text: Whenever you see “gallon,” establish whether it's US or imperial first — otherwise the error can reach 20%.
Trap 3: an ounce is both weight and volume

A fluid ounce (fl oz) is volume: 1 US fl oz ≈ 29.57 mL. An avoirdupois ounce (oz) is weight: 1 oz ≈ 28.35 g. The numbers are close but the meanings differ, and they aren't interchangeable across substances.
Trap 4: Fahrenheit and Celsius have different zeros

Temperature isn't a simple ratio conversion because the two scales have different zero points. The formula is °C = (°F − 32) × 5/9, and conversely °F = °C × 9/5 + 32. The usual error is multiplying without adding or subtracting 32.

For any unfamiliar unit, confirm three things: which system it belongs to, whether it's weight or volume, and whether identically named variants exist. Those three checks prevent most conversion errors.
Practical advice

Use a tool rather than mental math. Our unit converter covers length, weight, volume, and temperature, and cooking has a dedicated [cooking units converter](/cooking/cooking-units) better suited to real recipe quantities.

recipe-scaling-guide.title: How to Scale a Recipe Down from 8 Servings to 3
recipe-scaling-guide.excerpt: Ingredients scale linearly, but seasoning, spices, and baking time don't. Know the exceptions and your resized dish still tastes right.

blocks.text: To cut a recipe from 8 servings to 3, most people just multiply every ingredient by 3/8. That works most of the time — but for some ingredients it's a disaster.
What scales linearly

items: Main ingredients: meat, fish, vegetables, rice, and noodles scale directly.
Liquids: water, stock, and milk scale directly.
Sugar and oil: usually fine to scale proportionally.

blocks.text: Compute the base factor: target servings ÷ original servings. 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, so multiply each item by 0.375. The [Recipe Scaler](/cooking/recipe-scaler) does the arithmetic for you.
What does not scale simply

items: Salt and strong seasonings: taste isn't linear, so scale to about 70–80% first, then taste and adjust.
Spices and chili: also non-linear — start low, since you can always add more later.
Leaveners (baking powder, baking soda): they depend on pan geometry and chemical reactions; extreme scaling fails, so cook in batches.
Wine and vinegar: their flavor is potent, so scale to 50–75% and then adjust.

blocks.text: A practical rule: scale everything by the factor, but start salt, chili, and spices at 70%, then taste before serving. Add at the end if needed — never overshoot at the start.
Timing and pan size

With a smaller portion, baking time usually shortens, but not proportionally — check at about two-thirds of the original time, then extend. Less liquid also evaporates faster, so braises reduce sooner.
Match the pan to the volume: the same amount overflows a pan that's too small and scorches in one that's too large. Both depth and diameter affect heat transfer.
A unit-conversion shortcut

For awkward measures like “1/3 cup” or “2 tablespoons,” don't grind through the math. 1 cup = 16 tablespoons = 48 teaspoons: convert everything to the smallest unit, apply the factor, then convert back. The [cooking units converter](/cooking/cooking-units) handles this fastest.

cooking-measurement-standards.title: How Much Does a Cup of Flour Weigh? Why Baking Needs a Scale
cooking-measurement-standards.excerpt: One cook's cup of flour is 120 g, another's is 160 g. That uncertainty in volume measures is a classic cause of baking failures.

blocks.text: If you've ever followed a recipe and produced a brick-like cake, the recipe probably wasn't wrong — the question is how much “one cup” really was.
Where volume measurement goes wrong

items: How you fill it: flour scooped straight from the bag is denser than flour sifted and leveled — often by more than 20%.
Ingredient state: whether flour is sifted, sugar is packed, or butter is softened all change the volume.
Different cups: a “cup” isn't universal — about 240 mL in the US, about 200 mL in Japan.

blocks.text: Reference conversions

items: All-purpose flour: 1 cup ≈ 120–130 g (sifted and leveled)
Granulated sugar: 1 cup ≈ 200 g
Butter: 1 cup ≈ 227 g; 1 tablespoon ≈ 14 g
Milk/water: 1 cup ≈ 240 mL ≈ 240 g
Honey/syrup: 1 cup ≈ 340 g (far denser)

blocks.text: Treat these as approximations; brands and technique shift them. For precise conversion, use the [cooking units converter](/cooking/cooking-units).
Baking is chemistry, not improvisation. A 10% error in flour or liquid is enough to turn a tender cake dense.
Why weighing is better

A digital scale costs little and usually reads to 1 g. Weights are fully repeatable, unaffected by how you scoop, and let you share a recipe without ambiguity — which is why professional formulas are written in grams.
When cups are fine

Not every dish needs weighing. Stir-fries, stews, and soups are forgiving: volume measures are plenty and adjusting by feel is more flexible. Reserve the scale for baking, sauces, and desserts where ratios matter.

ratio-and-proportion-practical.title: Ratios and Proportions: From Mixing Drinks to Reading Maps
ratio-and-proportion-practical.excerpt: How do you dilute a 1:4 concentrate? What does a 1:10000 map mean? Ratios are the most practical — and most misread — math in daily life.

blocks.text: A ratio expresses the relationship between two quantities. It's simple enough to be overlooked, yet misusing it has real consequences, from undrinkable cordial to a wrong dose.
Two common notations

items: a:b — a relationship between two amounts, e.g. concentrate:water = 1:4.
a:b:c — a continued ratio across three or more amounts, e.g. concrete at 1:2:3.

blocks.text: The key point: 1:4 means 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water — a total of 5 parts, not 4. That is the most common mistake.
Everyday examples

items: Mixing drinks: for 500 mL at 1:4, concentrate = 500 ÷ 5 × 1 = 100 mL and water = 400 mL.
Map scale: 1:10000 means 1 cm on the map equals 10,000 cm — i.e. 100 m — on the ground.
Aspect ratio: 16:9 means the width is 16/9 of the height.
Diluting cleaner: 1:10 means 1 part product plus 10 parts water, giving 11 parts total.

blocks.text: A reliable check: add the parts of the ratio together. The total parts should match the final total quantity. If it doesn't, one term is wrong.
Converting ratios to percentages
A ratio converts to a percentage: in a:b, a's share is a ÷ (a + b). With a male-to-female ratio of 3:2, men are 3/5 = 60%. Conversely, 60% can be written as 3:2 or 60:40.
For complex cases, let the [Ratio Calculator](/math/ratio-calculator) handle the arithmetic, especially with three or more terms or when solving backwards.
One thing people mix up

A ratio is not the same as a rate. A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind and has no unit; a rate usually compares different kinds and carries a unit, like speed (km/h) or population density (people/km²). Confusing them produces dimensional errors.

how-much-house-can-you-afford.title: How Much House Can You Afford? Three Numbers the Bank Won't Volunteer
how-much-house-can-you-afford.excerpt: The amount a bank approves and the amount you can truly sustain are usually far apart. Three ratios tell you the safe number.

blocks.text: When a bank approves a mortgage it asks “can they repay?”, using income multiples and debt ratios. That's a ceiling, not the figure you should use. A sustainable home budget is something you calculate yourself.
Number one: the 28/36 rule

items: Housing costs under 28% of monthly income: mortgage payment, HOA fees, property tax, insurance.
Total debt under 36% of monthly income: add car loans, credit cards, consumer loans, and support obligations.

blocks.text: Example: with $30,000 monthly household income, housing is capped at $8,400 and total debt at $10,800. If you already pay $3,000 for a car, keep the mortgage under $7,800.
Number two: down payment plus hidden costs

A down payment is typically 20–30%, but that's far from your total cash need. Also budget for transfer tax (about 1–3%), a maintenance reserve, agent fees, renovation, appliances, and at least six months of payments in reserve.
A common mistake is pouring every saving into the down payment, leaving nothing for renovation or emergencies. Keep at least 10–15% of the purchase price in cash beyond the down payment.
Number three: the stress test
Before signing, recalculate the payment with rates 1–2 percentage points higher and see if you can still cope. If your budget only works at today's rate, it has no resistance to rate moves.
Compare payments with the [Mortgage Calculator](/finance/mortgage) across rates and terms, then model prepayment with the [Loan Calculator](/finance/loan).
Don't forget holding costs

items: HOA or management fees: charged by area and a real long-term expense.
Maintenance and renovation: homes need continuous investment as they age.
Commuting: a cheaper suburb carries time and transport costs worth pricing in.
Opportunity cost: what the down payment might have earned if invested.

blocks.text: The figure you reach after all of this is what you can genuinely afford. It usually sits 20–30% below what the bank would lend — and it's the budget you can live with comfortably.

protein-intake-how-much.title: How Much Protein Do You Need? Calculate by Body Weight
protein-intake-how-much.excerpt: Sedentary people, lifters, and older adults need very different amounts. Multiplying body weight by a factor is the most practical estimate.

blocks.text: Protein requirements vary more between individuals than almost any other nutrient. A sedentary office worker and someone who lifts five days a week may differ by a factor of two.
Reference ranges by body weight

items: Sedentary, no training: 0.8 g per kg — the floor for basic needs.
Moderately active: 1.0–1.2 g per kg.
Regular resistance training: 1.4–1.8 g per kg.
Intense training or cutting: 1.8–2.2 g per kg.

blocks.text: A 70 kg person who lifts three times a week needs roughly 98–126 g per day. The [Protein Calculator](/health/protein-calculator) gives you the number directly.
Why intake should rise during a cut

In a calorie deficit the body tends to break down muscle for energy. Higher protein protects muscle, increases satiety, and raises the thermic effect of food — digesting protein itself burns more calories. That's the core reason to raise protein while cutting.
Spreading it across meals

How well protein is used depends partly on the dose per meal. Roughly 25–40 g per meal is considered optimal for stimulating muscle protein synthesis. Spreading 120 g across three meals beats eating 100 g at dinner.
Rather than obsess over total grams, make sure each meal contains a quality protein source: eggs, lean meat, fish, soy products, or dairy.
When to be careful

People with impaired kidney function must limit protein under medical supervision and can't apply a generic factor. Source quality matters too: prefer complete animal proteins or well-combined plant proteins.
The [Macro Calculator](/health/macro-calculator) splits protein, carbs, and fat in one step, which is simpler than calculating each separately.

average-mean-median-mode.title: Averages Mislead: Choosing Between Mean, Median, and Mode
average-mean-median-mode.excerpt: Why does “average salary” always feel inflated? Because extreme values pull the mean. Pick the right statistic to see the data clearly.

blocks.text: Under any story about “average salary,” someone always says they feel averaged away. That feeling is often justified — the mean is extremely sensitive to outliers.
What the three statistics are

items: Mean: the sum of all values divided by the count. The most common, but heavily influenced by extremes.
Median: the middle value once everything is sorted. Unaffected by extremes.
Mode: the most frequent value. Best for categorical data.

blocks.text: A clear example

A company has 10 employees: nine earn $8,000 a month and the CEO earns $92,000. The mean is (9 × 8,000 + 92,000) ÷ 10 = $16,400, which sounds comfortable. The median is $8,000 — and that's the reality for most people there.
Whenever you read “average income,” ask: mean or median? For heavily right-skewed data like income or house prices, the median is almost always the more representative figure.
Which to use when

items: Mean: when the distribution is fairly even, with no extremes, and you want to use every value (e.g. average test scores).
Median: when there are outliers or clear skew (income, house prices, price growth).
Mode: for categorical data, such as the most popular color or the most common size.

blocks.text: Putting it into practice

The [Average Calculator](/math/average-calculator) computes these quickly. For larger sets or to see the shape of the distribution, pair it with the [Standard Deviation Calculator](/math/standard-deviation-calculator) — the same mean with a different standard deviation can describe completely different situations.
Build one habit with every statistic you read: ask how it was calculated, who was sampled, and whether outliers exist. Those three questions defuse most misleading numbers.

car-loan-total-cost.title: The True Cost of a Car Loan: Four Costs Beyond the Monthly Payment
car-loan-total-cost.excerpt: “Zero-interest financing” sounds like a bargain, but once you add fees, insurance, taxes, and depreciation, the real cost often exceeds expectations.

blocks.text: Car-loan advertising focuses almost entirely on the monthly payment — “just $80 a day.” But what decides affordability is total outlay, and the monthly payment is only part of it.
Four costs besides the monthly payment

items: Down payment: usually 20–30% of the price, and the largest single cash outlay.
Sales tax or registration tax: a one-off payment, often a meaningful share of the price.
Insurance: priciest in the first year, easing later, but recurring every year.
Arrangement or financing fees: charged by the lender, sometimes 2–3% of the loan.

blocks.text: The truth about “zero interest”

Zero- or low-interest offers usually recover the cost in one of two ways: higher arrangement fees, or forfeiting the cash rebate — you typically can't have both. Sometimes taking “a big cash rebate plus a normal-rate loan” is cheaper overall.
The only reliable way to compare two offers is to compute total outlay: down payment + all monthly payments + fees + interest − cash rebate. Don't let the monthly figure lead you.
Compare with a calculator

Enter both scenarios into the [Auto Loan Calculator](/finance/auto-loan) and compare total interest and total outlay. If a dealer gives you only the monthly figure and not the total, treat that as a warning sign.
Don't ignore depreciation

A car is a depreciating asset. A new one typically loses 10–20% of its value the moment it leaves the lot, with the steepest drop in the first three years. Finance a fast-depreciating car over five years and you can easily owe more than it's worth.

items: Keep the term short to avoid mismatching the depreciation curve.
Consider a one-to-three-year-old car that has passed the steepest depreciation.
Don't set the down payment too low, or you risk negative equity.

blocks.text: Finally, confirm with the [Loan Calculator](/finance/loan) that the payment sits within your debt ceiling — see the 36% total-debt rule in [How Much House Can You Afford](/blog/how-much-house-can-you-afford).

food-cost-per-serving.title: Cost per Serving: Is Cooking at Home Really Cheaper?
food-cost-per-serving.excerpt: Cooking at home is usually cheaper than eating out, but the gap depends on how you count. Ingredients, seasonings, and energy all belong in the total.

blocks.text: “Cooking at home saves money” is near-universal advice, but once you add seasonings, gas, electricity, and your time, the conclusion may surprise you. That doesn't mean cooking isn't worth it — it means the arithmetic deserves a look.
What a dish actually costs

items: Main ingredients: meat, vegetables, staples — priced by the amount used, not the whole package.
Seasonings: oil, salt, soy sauce, spices — small per use, but they add up over time.
Energy: gas or electricity, usually a small amount per cooking session.
Trim loss: peeling and trimming typically remove 10–30% of what you bought.

blocks.text: The [Food Cost Calculator](/cooking/food-cost) adds these up to show the true cost per serving.
A common mistake: counting only main ingredients and ignoring seasonings and energy. For a simple home-cooked dish, those can be 15–25% of the cost.
The bulk-buying trap

Larger packs have a lower unit price, but consider two things: will you finish it before it spoils, and what does storage cost? Saving money on a 5 kg bag of rice doesn't offset throwing half of it away.
When cooking really is cheaper

items: Cooking for several people: costs spread out, so more portions means better value.
Using seasonal produce: out-of-season vegetables can cost two to three times as much.
Dishes with simple seasoning: recipes built on expensive sauces and imported spices escalate fast.
Reusing leftovers: a whole chicken across two meals beats buying breast alone.

blocks.text: The value of your time

Strictly speaking, cooking time has a cost, though most people don't count it — for many, cooking is relaxation or family time. Whether to include it is a personal call. If your time is expensive, partly prepared ingredients such as pre-cut vegetables may cost more per kilo yet still be cheaper overall.

rounding-and-significant-figures.title: Why Rounding Is Sometimes Wrong: Significant Figures and Error Accumulation
rounding-and-significant-figures.excerpt: Round at every step and the final result drifts. Understanding error accumulation and banker's rounding makes your calculations trustworthy.

blocks.text: Rounding is the first rule taught in school, yet in chained calculations or large datasets, mechanical rounding introduces systematic bias and accumulated error.
Problem one: don't round intermediate steps

Compute 1.4 × 2.6 × 3.8, rounding to one decimal each step: 1.4 × 2.6 = 3.64 → 3.6, then 3.6 × 3.8 = 13.68 → 13.7. Computed directly, 1.4 × 2.6 × 3.8 = 13.832 → 13.8. Rounding mid-way shifted the result by 0.1.
A basic principle: round only at the final step. Keep at least one or two extra significant figures throughout.
Problem two: rounding has systematic bias
Digits 1–4 round down and 6–9 round up, which looks fair, but the treatment of 5 gives one extra case to rounding up. Across large datasets that makes results systematically too high.

Statistics more often uses “round half to even” (banker's rounding): below 5 rounds down, above 5 rounds up, and exactly 5 goes to the nearest even number. Over many values, positive and negative biases cancel out.

items: 2.5 → 2 (toward the even number)
3.5 → 4 (toward the even number)

blocks.text: What significant figures are

Significant figures are the digits counted from the first non-zero digit, and they express the precision of a measurement or calculation. 0.0052 has two significant figures; 5.20 has three. A trailing zero isn't decorative — it says that zero was actually measured.
Rules of thumb: for addition and subtraction, match the fewest decimal places; for multiplication and division, match the fewest significant figures.
Using it day to day

The [Rounding Calculator](/math/rounding-calculator) handles a variety of rounding needs. Be especially careful with financial data: currency calculations typically specify two decimals, and you should round the final result rather than every intermediate amount.

sleep-cycles-when-to-wake.title: Sleep Cycles and Wake Times: Why 8 Hours Can Still Leave You Groggy
sleep-cycles-when-to-wake.excerpt: Sleep runs in roughly 90-minute cycles. Waking from deep sleep leaves you foggy even after enough hours. Timing your wake-up helps.

blocks.text: Sometimes eight hours leaves you groggy, while six and a half leaves you sharp. The difference is usually not total hours but which stage of the sleep cycle you wake from.
What a sleep cycle is

Sleep isn't a uniform state; it cycles in roughly 90-minute blocks containing light sleep, deep sleep, and REM sleep. Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night, REM the second. Being woken from deep sleep produces noticeable sleep inertia and grogginess.
How to time your wake-up

Since a cycle lasts about 90 minutes, aim for a total close to a whole number of cycles and wake at a cycle boundary. Targeting 7.5 hours (5 cycles) or 6 hours (4 cycles) usually leaves you clearer than 8 hours.

items: 6 hours = 4 cycles
7.5 hours = 5 cycles
9 hours = 6 cycles

blocks.text: Falling asleep usually takes another 10–20 minutes, so allow for that when counting back from your wake time. The [Sleep Calculator](/health/sleep-calculator) works out suitable bedtimes and wake times directly.
Cycle length varies between people; 90 minutes is an average. If 7.5 hours still leaves you tired, adjust by 15 minutes to find your own rhythm.
Matters more than duration

items: Regularity: sleeping and waking at roughly the same times daily beats occasional catch-up sleep.
Sleep pressure: enough waking time and physical activity during the day improves sleep quality.
Light: natural light in the morning and dimmer light before bed stabilize your circadian rhythm.
Alcohol: it speeds sleep onset but seriously disrupts sleep architecture in the second half of the night.

blocks.text: Don't over-trust the cycle

Cycle timing is a useful guide, not a cure-all. If you regularly wake exhausted, feel sleepy by day, or snore heavily, that may point to something like sleep apnea, which needs a doctor rather than a schedule tweak. Cycle math fixes when you wake, not the quality of the sleep itself.

home.intro: Baike Calc is a free online toolkit with 198 calculators and converters across 19 categories, including math, finance, health, image processing, engineering, and networking. Every calculation runs locally in your browser: nothing you type is uploaded to a server, and no account is required to use any tool. Each tool page includes step-by-step instructions, an explanation of the underlying formula, and a set of frequently asked questions, so you can understand how a result is derived instead of just reading a number. Whether you are a student, an engineer, a finance professional, or someone who just needs a quick figure, you will find a tool that fits.

faq.q: Are these tools really free?
faq.a: Yes. Every calculator and converter on this site is free to use, with no account required and no daily usage cap. The site is supported by advertising, which covers hosting and development costs but never affects the accuracy of any result.

faq.q: Is the data I type uploaded to a server?
faq.a: No. For the vast majority of tools the calculation runs entirely in your browser and your input never leaves your device. A small number of tools that need external data, such as live exchange rates, request it from public sources, but they do not record or store the specific values you enter.

faq.q: Can I use the results for tax filings or medical decisions?
faq.a: No. The tools provide estimates for general reference. Financial results are not a substitute for professional tax advice, and health results are not a diagnosis. For decisions that matter, consult a licensed professional.

guide.step1: Enter the values you want to calculate in the input fields at the top of the page.
guide.step2: Switch units or adjust the options as needed. Most tools update the result as you type.
guide.step3: Read the result area, then use the explanation and the questions below to understand what it means and where it applies.
guide.fallbackIntro: {name} is a free online calculator. {description} Everything runs locally in your browser, so the values you enter are never uploaded to a server.
guide.fallbackA1: Results follow published standard formulas and conversion factors and are accurate enough for everyday use. For professional purposes such as tax filings, medical diagnosis or engineering design, rely on the authoritative standard or a licensed professional instead.
guide.fallbackQ2: Is the data I enter stored anywhere?
guide.fallbackA2: No. The calculation happens inside your browser and your input is never uploaded. Once you close the page the values are gone, and we have no way to see what you entered.
guide.fallbackQ3: Do I need to register or pay to use this?
guide.fallbackA3: No. Every tool on this site is free, no account is required, and there is no daily usage limit.
